extractionNotes: Extracted via pdftotext -layout in sequential chunks covering the full 217-page document. Printed page footers run 2 pages behind the raw PDF page index throughout the document (e.g. raw PDF page 25 = printed page 23, footer 'ENGLISH LANGUAGE | 23'); pdfPageIndex values in this file = printed page + 2, confirmed by cross-referencing footer text against the raw -f/-l ranges requested during extraction.

Document structure: 5 fixed Strands (1. Oral Language, 2. Reading, 3. Grammar (Usage), 4. Writing, 5. Literature) repeated once per Year (SHS 1/2/3). Each Strand's subStrands[] array in this file concatenates all three years' instances of that Strand's sub-strands in document order (Year 1 sub-strands first, then Year 2, then Year 3), matching the convention used in geography.json/other completed subject files, not the alternate per-year-Strand-object shape.

Scope and Sequence summary table (PDF raw page 23, printed page 21) gives Overall Totals (SHS 1-3): 46 Content Standards, 58 Learning Outcomes, 102 Learning Indicators. The same table's per-Strand/per-Sub-Strand/per-Year cell values are garbled by column-collision in the -layout text extraction (e.g. 'English Speech Sounds 1 13 126' cannot be reliably parsed into separate CS/LO/LI digits per cell) -- only the clean bottom-line overall totals and the per-Year row totals (Year1: 15 CS/23 LO/43 LI; Year2: 16 CS/19 LO/34 LI; Year3: 15 CS/16 LO/25 LI) were extractable with confidence.

CONFIRMED IN BODY (not just inferred from the summary table): Learning Outcomes outnumber Content Standards in this subject because several Content Standards are genuinely shared by multiple sibling Learning Outcomes within the same sub-strand (the source prints all of a sub-strand's LOs together in a 'Learning Outcomes' table, followed by fewer Content-Standard/Learning-Indicator blocks than there are LOs). Per the canonical schema, each printed Content Standard is nested under exactly ONE Learning Outcome (its closest topical match by content, to avoid inflating node counts via duplication); a reviewNote is attached to every such Content Standard identifying the sibling Learning Outcome(s) in the same sub-strand whose content it also covers, so the many-to-one relationship is preserved as documentation without double-counting nodes. Confirmed cases: Year 1 Strand 3 Sub-Strand 1 (GRAMMAR): 5 LOs, 2 CS -- CS.1 (nouns/pronouns/adjectives/verbs/minor word classes) matches LO.1 (word classes); CS.2 (subject-predicate/sentence elements/compound sentences/clauses/phrases) is attached to LO.2 but its Learning Indicators also cover the topics of LO.3, LO.4 and LO.5. Year 1 Strand 5 Sub-Strand 1 (NARRATIVE, DRAMA, POETRY): 5 LOs, 1 CS (6 LIs) -- the single CS.1 is attached to LO.1 but covers all of LO.1-LO.5's topics (genres, characterisation, monologue/dialogue, plot sequence, African poem themes).

In pairs/groups, learners listen to and identify the English short vowels in sample-spoken texts (e.g. tape recordings, podcast, radio, read aloud exercises, tongue twisters, YouTube videos on vowel sounds etc.). Conversations/Interviews: In pairs and groups, learners use short vowel sounds in words and connected speech through conversations/interviews, skits (short plays), etc.

learningIndicators.description: Recognise the main ideas in level-appropriate oral texts.
pedagogicalExemplars: Think-Pair-Share Activity (e.g., Peer/pair work, small group work): Learners listen to a level appropriate oral text (audio recordings, videos, stories, narrations, etc.) and discuss the main ideas in pairs. Selected texts should reflect varied cultural backgrounds, values, interests and affiliations. Learners collaborate and communicate their ideas in a cordial manner, deliberating on questions such as: What is/are the speaker(s) referring to? What does/do the speaker(s) want me to know? What did you learn from the passage (e.g.: theme, character, moral lesson)? What are the key ideas in the text? What will you suggest as a suitable title for the text and why?

Example 2: Learners, individually or in pairs, identify the key information from the oral text/communication, summarise in their own words what the text is about by focusing on the key ideas identified, and suggest a suitable title for the narrative.
Example 3: Learners role-play the passage to reinforce the lesson.

learningIndicators.description: Differentiate between important ideas and unimportant ideas in level appropriate oral texts.
pedagogicalExemplars: Experiential Learning: Learners talk about their experiences relating to information presented in an oral text, reflect on the ideas and distinguish between the more and less important ideas in the text. Through this, learners develop an enquiry-based approach to continuous learning.

Use strategies such as: Word chain (i.e., repetition of similar words or sequences), sorting of word cards, group work to differentiate the main ideas from the subsidiary ones. Example: In groups, learners sort important and less important information written on sheets of paper, and discuss why some ideas are considered as main ideas and others as less important information.

Note: Pay attention to the beginning and end of a conversation; paralinguistic features (tone of voice, stressed/unstressed words) and non-verbal cues (gestures, facial expressions, etc.); speakers' use of descriptive terms and examples which normally introduce subsidiary ideas in communication; speaking cues (e.g. Today we will focus on..., the story is about..., Let's move on to..., In other words..., the result of this is..., etc.).

learningIndicators.description: Use language appropriately in different speech situations (e.g., formal and informal).
pedagogicalExemplars: Talk for learning (TfL): Learners, in mixed-ability groups, engage in practical demonstrations of everyday discourse and group conversations around a particular topic to enable them, collaboratively, identify and use specific registers and expressions. E.g., Group discussions on the impact of Covid-19 on students' academic life or asking for direction, requesting a favour, describing a market scene, attending a job interview, asking questions in class, etc. Selected topics should appeal to learners from diverse backgrounds (ethnic, religious, cultural) and involve both males and females.

Class Activity: Learners watch short videos/read short stories based on a given speech context (e.g., formal, semi-formal or informal contexts). In small groups, exhibiting the values of tolerance through exploratory talk, learners discuss a video/story, give reasons for what participants in the video or story said and compile a list of useful expressions used in the video/story. Learners may use discussion topics such as: What is happening in the video/story? Who are the participants? Who are the intended audience of the video/story? Where is the conversation taking place? What lesson is the video/story teaching us? Learners then role-play the video/story, paying attention to the language/communicative strategies employed by the characters.

Learners in their groups then role-play the short scenario on a given speech act. Through a class discussion, learners discuss their choices in terms of appropriate ways of expressing the acts (direct/indirect) and their responses to the speech acts.

learningIndicators.description: Use diphthongs (closing and centring) in connected speech.
pedagogicalExemplars: Collaborative Learning: Learners in attainment groups, work collaboratively to identify the features of diphthongs and use them effectively in words and in connected speech. Learners critically assess the sound combination of diphthongs in English and creatively blend them into meaningful words, communicating with clarity and confidence, mindful of the unique qualities of each sound while tolerating their peers' individual differences in articulation.

Examples: in groups, learners brainstorm on words that contain closing diphthongs and centring diphthongs (e.g. bake, say, sail, pain; boy, foil, poise; air, tear, bear). In pairs, learners use words containing the diphthongs to form sentences (e.g. 'I may break the cage.' 'Both girls and boys play with toys.'). Using a jigsaw game, learners in their groups find appropriate sounds to complete words (e.g. hoist, bow, jewel, growl, boy, lawn, audio). Learners have the opportunity to communicate freely among themselves in the groups as they share opinions.

E.g., in groups, learners brainstorm on words that contain triphthongs (e.g. layer, liar, fire, loyal, royal, lower, mower, power, hour). Learners then, in pairs, use the words to form sentences (e.g. 'Loyalty is a virtue.' 'It is bad to be a liar.').

learningIndicators.description: Use consonant sounds (affricates and approximants) in connected speech.

Learners then, in their convenient groups, work collaboratively, using the sounds and paying attention to their peers' unique individual differences in articulating the sounds in connected speech.

Think-Pair-Share: Alternatively, in their attainment groups, learners may use think-pair-share to practise the pronunciation of the consonant sounds in the words in a given passage. Learners then in pairs, form sentences with words containing the consonant sounds (e.g. church, judge, water, red, yes). E.g. The cheerleader read the well-written letter yesterday. Learners finally create dialogues with words containing the consonant sounds to consolidate their new knowledge and improve upon their communication skills, communicating with clarity and confidence.

learningIndicators.description: Identify patterns of consonant clusters occurring at syllable initial and final positions in connected speech.
pedagogicalExemplars: Collaborative Learning: In mixed-ability groups, learners brainstorm on common consonant clusters occurring at syllable initial and final positions, paying attention to patterns of consonant cluster formation and using them in everyday interaction with clarity and confidence. Examples: two-consonant clusters at initial position (br-, fr-, gr-, cl-, cr-, sc/sk-, sl-, tr-) and final position (-sk, -x/ks, -st, -nk); three-consonant clusters at initial position (scr-, spr-, str-, spl-).

In convenient mixed ability groups, learners identify and/or generate words containing the consonant clusters. In group class presentations, learners articulate consonants and consonant clusters appropriately through language games (e.g. tongue twisters). Word Search: learners in their groups search for as many words that match given consonant cluster sounds within a given number of minutes. Through pair/group activities, learners cultivate team spirit, tolerance, apply critical thinking and work collaboratively.

learningIndicators.description: Pronounce words containing consonant clusters accurately in connected speech, including consonant clusters with silent sounds (e.g.: subtle, listen, comb, etc.).
pedagogicalExemplars: Independent Learning: Individually, learners use the identified words containing consonant clusters in speech, paying particular attention to common mispronunciation problems involving consonant clusters, and are critical in identifying appropriate words.

Think-Pair-Share: Examples of common mispronunciations - changing the order of consonant sounds (e.g. saying /ssk/ for /sks/ = six); leaving out a sound in the cluster (e.g. access, success); adding an extra sound or inserting a vowel in between the cluster (e.g. silk, square). In pairs, learners take turns to articulate the sounds accurately and to avoid the commonly misappropriated consonant clusters.

Collaborative Learning: In mixed ability groups, learners work collaboratively to identify words containing consonant clusters having one of the consonant sounds silent (e.g. subtle, listen, comb). Learners, in groups, take turns to pronounce the words with silent consonants appropriately in speech.

learningIndicators.description: Recognise the purpose of varied oral communication.
pedagogicalExemplars: Collaborative Learning: In their mixed ability groups, learners work collaboratively to recognise the purpose of varied oral communication, appreciating their individual capabilities and developing tolerance for others' points of view. E.g., learners individually listen to a level appropriate text and identify the purpose of the communication (to inform, to express one's feelings, to persuade, etc.).

Learners in groups discuss the purpose of the text. Using a Round-robin technique, learners ensure that each member of the group takes turns to express their ideas on the purpose of the communication so that no particular learner monopolises the discussion. Learners take turns to share ideas agreed on in the group with members of other groups or the whole class.

pedagogicalExemplars: Initiating Talk for Learning: Learners in their mixed ability groups extract relevant information from texts by identifying a speaker's intended meaning from a sample oral text, communicating effectively with others (both male and female), valuing others' perspectives in interaction and in adult life. E.g., Think-pair-share activity: learners in pairs brainstorm a speaker's intended meaning (to request, command, declare, offer, promise, warn/caution, etc.) of a particular message in conversation, then interpret the purpose of the intended meaning of the speaker in relation to the context of speaking, finally sharing ideas with the larger group to reach a consensus.

pedagogicalExemplars: Collaborative Learning: Learners work in their mixed-ability groups to reflect on other properties of speech (e.g., stress), which extend beyond the individual sound segments (vowels and consonants). With appropriate examples, learners come to understand how stress (placing prominence) on certain words or parts of a word (syllable) aids in communicating meaningfully, developing team spirit and embracing diversity.

Class Discussion: Learners listen to a model text uttered in level tone with no emphasis on content or main words, reflect and record observations (e.g. does the reading sound monotonous, right, natural?). Learners listen to a second reading with emphasis on content/main words and note reactions. In pairs, learners identify stressed vs. unstressed words (content words are stressed, grammatical words are not). In pairs, learners refer to reference materials (e.g. dictionary) to observe stress marking on disyllabic/polysyllabic words. In groups, learners listen to model oral texts to observe stress marking in natural conversation. In pairs, learners take turns reading model texts, emphasising stressed syllables/words. Individually, learners record their own reading and play it back, attending to their articulation of stressed/unstressed syllables, content and grammatical words, appreciating different competencies and communicating effectively.

Talk for Learning Approaches (TFL): e.g., Brainstorming, talking circles, partner talk, think-pair-share, etc.

Skimming: In convenient mixed gender/ability groups, learners collaborate to survey texts for the general idea, using features such as title, illustrations, boldface words, headings and subheadings, topic sentences and concluding sentences to examine texts for the gist of the story, and use questions at the end of texts to derive the gist. Learners read and interpret texts from familiar backgrounds and connect the messages to their personal lives. In groups, learners download (or search newspapers for) positive stories from social media about familiar and popular personalities in the country and use the text to practise scanning and skimming in class.

learningIndicators.description: Use a variety of text comprehension strategies to analyse fiction and non-fiction texts.
pedagogicalExemplars: Think-Pair-Share/Group Work: In pairs/groups, learners discuss the importance of prediction in real life situations and link it with its role in enhancing reading comprehension. Learners listen to a simple but interesting text read aloud and try to make logical predictions at the beginning, middle, and end of the text (fiction), supporting predictions with evidence from the text. In mixed ability reading groups (of not more than five members), learners work collaboratively under their group leaders to read other interesting texts, predicting, reviewing and re-predicting the story till they come to an end. Groups choose delegates to present their work to the class and critically critique/peer review each group's presentation. Model how to fill the prediction forms at the beginning, middle and end of the texts. Learners work collaboratively to use titles, illustrations, bold print, italics, headings, subheadings and other text features to predict non-fiction texts. Leadership roles should be assigned to both male and female members.

Group Work/Collaborative Learning: Learners use KWL, DRTA and chunking strategies to interpret advanced texts. Know, Want-to-know, and Learned (KWL): Learners work in mixed gender and mixed ability groups to brainstorm what they know and want to know about titles of given texts, fill the K and W columns of the KWL sheet, then read the text and fill their L column with what they have learned, presenting their KWL sheets to the class explaining what happened at each stage of the reading.

Directed Reading Thinking Activity (DRTA)/Chunking: Breaking texts into smaller parts for easier reading and comprehension. Using probing questions, learners' background knowledge about the title of a text is activated and they predict what the text will be about. At the reading stage, learners read the text in small sections; at the end of each chunk, questions are asked and if learners cannot answer correctly, they are directed to re-read portions of the text related to the answer, working in pairs to locate the answer.

Additional Metacognitive Practices: Learners read text and use text markers (metacognitive markers) to indicate their impressions about parts of the text; use a second reading to circle/write down unknown words and find their meanings in context; underline ideas relating to other texts, their personal lives, or experiences elsewhere in the world; re-read portions to answer comprehension questions; create mental pictures of what is read; work in groups to apply their knowledge of metacognitive strategies like KWL, DRA and DRTA/Chunking to enhance comprehension. Groups share their work with the class and critique one another's work.

Groups write the story on a flip chart and post them on the classroom walls for a gallery walk. learningIndicators.description: Apply innovative strategies in summarising short but familiar stories.
pedagogicalExemplars: Group Work/Collaborative Learning: Learners use the SWBST Strategy to summarise a variety of short fiction (prose and drama). Note: SWBST means Somebody, Wants, But, So, Then. In small mixed ability and mixed gender groups, learners listen to a story read aloud to the class. They work collaboratively to summarise the story heard by critically discussing and answering the SWBST questions: Somebody - Who is the main character? Want - What does the main character want or want to do? But - What is the problem, or why can't the main character get what she or he wants? So - How does the main character solve the problem? Then - What was the resolution? In mixed-ability/mixed gender groups, learners apply the SWBST strategy to familiar stories (e.g., Cinderella story). Encourage learners to tolerate and accept one another's views as well as connect the stories to their personal lives, learning to identify social injustice and advocating for change.

The 5Ws: Learners use 'The 5Ws' strategy: Who, When, Where, Why and How to summarise stories. In groups/in pairs, learners work on given texts, responding to the 5Ws; there could be 5 groups, each responding to one 'W'. Ensure that each group can work on all the paragraphs in the passage. Selected texts should be gender responsive and reflect cultural settings that learners can identify with in their discussions.

learningIndicators.description: Explore the knowledge of grammatical structures of language and context clues to interpret complex structures in text.
pedagogicalExemplars: Group Work/Collaborative Learning: Learners identify complex grammatical structures that pose difficulty in text interpretation, working in mixed ability groups to collaboratively read given texts and identify problematic structures. Text should be devoid of gender bias language. Learners work in mixed ability/mixed gender groups to break complex structures into simple sentences for better interpretation; text difficulty should be differentiated to enable struggling readers to participate.

Talk for Learning (TFL) / Initiating Talk for Learning: Learners use context clues to interpret given words and phrases, working collaboratively in mixed ability/mixed gender groups to critically discuss the parts of speech/function of certain words or phrases in the structure of given sentences (e.g., 'The Ghanaian footballers are skilful' - 'Ghanaian' modifying footballers as an adjective).

Learners do vocabulary consolidation activities to promote active engagement with vocabulary, working collaboratively in small mixed ability groups to practise using context clues, word parts (e.g., prefixes) and reference aids (dictionary, glossary, thesauruses) to analyse texts and broaden comprehension of vocabulary. Learners carry out a project to find other means of understanding vocabulary in context.

learningIndicators.description: Read and analyse a variety of level-appropriate texts for enjoyment.
pedagogicalExemplars: Individual Learning: Learners select and read books individually for enjoyment; book choice should reflect particular topics/issues. Learners use the blurb of fiction texts as a guide for selecting books for individual reading.

Group Work/Collaborative Learning: In mixed gender groups, learners read their texts silently and share what they have read with group members. The group works collaboratively and critically to select the most interesting story, reads it again and fills in a reporting worksheet.

Gallery Walk: Groups paste their reports on the classroom walls for a gallery walk to help learners embrace diversity and understand their capabilities in relation to others; each group gives reasons for their choice of text; learners critique the stories and identify the overall most interesting text. learningIndicators.description: Read a variety of level-appropriate texts fluently.
pedagogicalExemplars: Group Work/Collaborative Learning and Talk for Learning: Learners brainstorm the importance of reading fluently. In mixed ability/mixed gender groups, learners listen to the teacher read the same text in two different ways (less-fluently and fluently) and critically discuss which reading is understood better and why. Learners listen to the teacher discuss how to read fluently (read words automatically, read in meaningful chunks, pause appropriately), watch videos/demonstrations, discuss and set targets for their individual reading. The class models how to calculate a reader's fluency within a minute; in groups, learners take turns to read for members to calculate their individual fluency rate.

Talk for Learning/Pair Work: Learners engage in a variety of fluency activities (Choral Reading, Partner Reading, Tape-Assisted Reading, Readers' Theatre using scripts derived from books rich in dialogue e.g. Core Literature-in-English Drama set books) to make reading fun and improve fluency rate.

Texts must be gender and inclusion responsive, avoiding gender bias language.

In pairs, learners take turns playing 'Coach' and 'Player' in shrinking paragraphs into main points; if a player gets it wrong, the Coach asks them to skim the paragraph again and answer a second time.

Structuring Talk for Learning: Pairs join another pair to think critically about how to state the main ideas of a given paragraph in 10 words or less. Group presenter roles should be assigned to both male and female members. Groups share their work with the class for feedback.

In mixed ability/mixed gender pairs, learners read short pieces of text and work collaboratively to answer who, what, when, where, why and how questions, then join another pair to condense their answers into a one-sentence summary. Groups share their one-sentence summaries with the class for peer feedback. Learners are tasked to search for other interactive ways of summarising texts.

pedagogicalExemplars: Group Work/Collaborative Learning - Reciprocal Teaching as a Collaborative Strategy: Learners work collaboratively to read a text or section of a text together as a class, starting with a short, simple-structure text and moving to complex and lengthy texts. In mixed ability/mixed gender groups of four, each member is assigned a role: The Questioner (formulates two questions), The Clarifier (finds two unknown words/ideas), The Summarizer (draws a picture representing the main idea), The Predictor (predicts what might happen next). Learners complete a Reciprocal Teaching Worksheet independently, then work collaboratively to discuss and complete the second part: answer the Questioner's questions, define/explain the Clarifier's unknown words, the Summariser shares and the group draws a similar picture and writes a summary, the Predictor reveals their prediction and the group finds supporting evidence. Learners share their work for peer feedback.

learningIndicators.description: Use nouns accurately in speech and writing.
pedagogicalExemplars: Brainstorming: Learners work in mixed ability groups ensuring collaboration and respecting one another's views to identify nouns in context and use them in speech and writing.
Task-Based Learning: Learners in mixed ability groups brainstorm the concept of nouns, encouraging one another to define and give examples taking into consideration their cultural backgrounds.
Think-Pair-Share: Learners use previous examples given in the brainstorming session to identify the noun forms as they think in pairs and share ideas, supporting the involvement of all.

Group Work: Learners in mixed ability groups collaboratively classify nouns from selected passages into noun types/forms: Common Nouns (chair, book), Proper Nouns (Adwoa, Musa, Ghana, Lake Volta, Canada), Concrete Nouns (window, projector, computer, bottle), Abstract Nouns (love, kindness, honesty), Count Nouns (pen-pens, book-books), Non-Count Nouns (water, oil, sugar), Collective Nouns (children, family, police, clergy). Note: Teacher guides learners to identify regular and irregular nouns (e.g. pen/pens vs. man/men, ox/oxen, sheep/sheep).

Genitive Forms of Nouns / Games: Learners in gender groupings use games to form genitives of nouns appropriately in speech and writing, e.g. Building on What Others Say (chain game) for the 's' genitive; adding 's' to regular nouns to show possession (Akwasi's bag); adding the apostrophe to regular plural nouns (the boys' dormitory); adding the apostrophe to nouns ending in 's' (Abass' book, Rawlings', James's bag); adding 'of' to the noun phrase (the title of the poem).
Conversation Drills: Using conversation drills, learners (in pairs, groups, whole class, dialogues etc) use the 's' genitive and the 'of' form in sentences.

KWL (What I know-What I want to know-What I have Learnt): Learners play the KWL game in their mixed ability pairs to identify and use plural noun forms in selected passages/texts ensuring collaboration and respect for one another's views.

Learners in their mixed ability groups creatively explore the use of pronouns from varieties of texts respecting varieties of views.

Types covered: 1. Personal Pronoun (I, you, she, he, it, we, they, me, us, them). 2. Possessives (mine, yours, his, hers, ours, theirs). 3. Relative pronouns (who, whom, which, what, that). 4. Interrogatives (who, whom, what, which, whose). 5. Reflexives (myself, yourself, itself, herself, himself, ourselves, themselves). 6. Demonstratives (this, that, these, those).

Examples of use: directly before nouns (Amuzu is an amazing footballer); with the verb 'to be' to describe the subject (Fatima is very intelligent); with sense (sensory) verbs (the food tastes awful); verbs of appearance modifying nouns before the verb (Papa Minka seemed very upset).

Examples: Base(V) infinitive/-s form (sit-sits, buy-buys); Past -ed1 (called, drank); Participle (V+ing) (calling, drinking), Participle (V+ed2) (called, drunk); Regular verbs (talk, want, advise, weed); Irregular verbs (come, eat, go, get, say, write). Use verbs correctly in appropriate tense forms: Present Tense (Simple, Progressive, Perfect, Perfect Progressive), Past Tense (Simple, Progressive, Perfect, Perfect Progressive). The primary auxiliaries are: do, have, be. Use modal auxiliaries can/could, will/would, may/might, must, need, etc.
Note: Use demonstration/role play/dialogue to distinguish forms and other uses of Tense and Aspect; explanation of relationship between time, tense and aspect, and the forms of the Present Tense.

Preposition - use in sentences (e.g. consist of, in front of, on behalf of, in view of, in spite of, due to, near to, because of, by means of, by dint of); complex prepositions to express place, time, reason and concession.

Determiners: Articles (the, a, an); Possessives (our, your, my, their, her, his - e.g. Her car is over there); Demonstratives (that, this, there, these, those). Use determiners in sentences and paragraphs (e.g. That cat is very fat. An apple fell from the tree. Is your coffee on the counter?).

Note: Active - S V O (e.g. 'The girl swept the room.'); Passive - Verb be + past participle of main verb (e.g. 'The room was swept by the girl.'). The passive voice is used when the agent is not mentioned (e.g. 'My book has been stolen.'). Some expressions are always in the passive (e.g. 'I was born in 1960.'). Conversion of active into passive: active subject becomes passive agent, active object becomes passive subject (e.g. 'Pearl sewed the dress.' -> 'The dress was sewn by Pearl.'); the preposition 'by' is introduced before the agent. Use of passive voice: for writing reports, minutes etc.
